questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of rash and fever. He had returned 1 week before his symptoms began from a 4-week holiday in Nigeria visiting family. He worked as a postal worker. On examination his temperature was 38.7°C, his heart rate was 110 beats/minute, and his blood pressure was 110/64 mmHg. He had a vesicular rash affecting predominantly his trunk, with many vesicles that were easy to burst. There are some macular lesions as well as the vesicles.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chickenpox The characteristic rash, with vesicles affecting the trunk as opposed to extremities, and easy to slough off, indicates chickenpox as the likely diagnosis. He could have been exposed to monkeypox in Nigeria as there are ongoing outbreaks, but the rash in monkeypox largely affects the face and extremities. He is also a postal worker, an occupational risk factor for exposure to bioterrorist acts, but the rash distribution, and the lesions at differing stages of development are against a diagnosis such as smallpox.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q46

questions.stem: A 54-year-old pet store owner presented with 4 days of fever and headache, and 2 days of a rash that had started on his face and spread outward. On examination, he had a macular rash over his face and distal extremities, with only a few lesions on his abdomen and back. His temperature was 38.3°C. He had widespread lymphadenopathy. Examination of his cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations was unremarkable. He was admitted for observation and investigation. Over the next few days the rash evolved from macules to vesicles to pustules. The fever persisted for 8 days in total, the rash for 12 days. Electron microscopy of lesion biopsy:
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Intrauterine death The diagnosis of monkeypox infection requires clinical (rash), epidemiologic (equatorial Africa), and laboratory (the presence of genomic DNA or brick-shaped virions in scab material) findings. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)

questions.question: List 1 infection (causative organism not required) under each category that causes an eschar.

parts_raw.text: List 1 infection (causative organism not required) under each category that cause an eschar - Rickettsial

questions.model_answer: a) Rickettsial: African tick-bite fever (Rickettsia africae) - alternatives include scrub typhus, Mediterranean spotted fever, rickettsialpox. b) Bacterial (non-rickettsial): Ulceroglandular tularaemia (Francisella tularensis); alternatively cutaneous anthrax or plague. c) Virus: Orthopoxvirus infection - smallpox/vaccinia (crusting eschar).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only part a) is grounded in this chapter (Table 185.3 lists rickettsioses with eschar). Bacterial and viral eschar causes are from standard ID sources, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Rickettsial: Scrub typhus, murine typhus, epidemic typhus, african tick bite fever (Orientia tsutsugamushi, rickettsia africae). Bacterial (non-rickettsial): Tularemia, plague (Francisella tularensis, yersinia pestis); Ecthyma (pseudomonas). Virus: Smallpox, vaccinia

questions.question: Antiviral therapy for mpox (monkeypox virus infection).

parts.text: Which antiviral is Health Canada approved for mpox?

parts_raw.text: Which antiviral is health Canada approved for Mpox

questions.model_answer: a) Tecovirimat (TPOXX/ST-246) - the orally bioavailable orthopoxvirus egress inhibitor; it is the antiviral used for mpox in Canada (approved for orthopoxvirus disease including mpox; Mandell records the 2018 FDA approval for smallpox). Cidofovir/brincidofovir and VIGIV remain unlicensed alternatives.
questions.beyond_mandell: Health Canada authorized tecovirimat (TPOXX) in 2022-2023; prior to that it was supplied through the Special Access Programme. Mandell 9e documents only the 2018 US FDA smallpox approval.

questions.question: COVID-19 (viruses).

parts.text: Name three proteins aside from the spike protein.
Name one approved treatment for mpox.
Describe remdesivir treatment efficacy as per animal models.

parts_raw.text: Remdesivir treatment efficacy as per animal models

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Envelope (E). (2) Membrane (M). (3) Nucleocapsid (N).
b) Tecovirimat (TPOXX), an inhibitor of the orthopoxvirus VP37 envelope-wrapping protein required for formation and dissemination of infectious virions. (Brincidofovir/cidofovir are alternatives.)
c) In rhesus macaques inoculated with SARS-CoV-2 and treated with remdesivir 12 hours after inoculation, treated animals had no or markedly reduced respiratory disease (only 1 of 6 with dyspnea vs all untreated controls), lower lung viral loads and less severe lung pathology, though no reduction in upper respiratory shedding. Similar prophylactic and early-therapeutic benefit was shown in MERS-CoV macaque and mouse models and in Ebola virus-infected macaques.

cohort_answer.text:
3 proteins: Envelope; Membrane; Nucleocapsid.
Approved treatment for Mpox: Tecovirimat (Tpoxx) - potent inhibitor of an orthopoxvirus protein required for formation of an infectious virus particle, essential for dissemination within an infected host. (Cidofovir has in vitro activity against monkeypox virus and shown effective against lethal monkeypox virus challenge in animal models.)
Remdesivir efficacy in animal models: In a study of 12 macaques, 6 treated with Remdesivir and 6 not; of the 6 treated only 1 developed dyspnea vs all of the untreated. Outpatient treatment: 4/246 (1.6%) treated arm vs 21/252 (8.3%) placebo arm required a medical visit. Inpatient treatment: 1062 randomized to remdesivir or placebo; median recovery time 10 days vs 15 days; mortality at day 15: 6.7% vs 11.9%; mortality at day 29: 11.4% vs 15.2%.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man who has sex with multiple men presents with this rash: [image-based question: rash in an MSM patient]
questions.question_raw: A 24 year old man who had sex with multiple men presents with this rash: [image-based question: rash in an MSM patient]

parts.text: What is ONE off-label treatment for this condition?
What is the gene target or viral protein target of this treatment?

parts_raw.text: What is ONE off-label treatment for this condition?
What is the gene target or viral protein target of this treatment?

questions.model_answer:
a) Mpox (human monkeypox virus infection), an orthopoxvirus producing a firm, deep-seated, umbilicated vesiculopustular rash with lesions in the same stage, fever and prominent lymphadenopathy; in this MSM context it is sexually transmitted with anogenital lesions.
b) Tecovirimat (ST-246/TPOXX) - licensed for smallpox and used off-label for mpox (alternatives: cidofovir or brincidofovir, also off-label).
c) Tecovirimat targets the orthopoxvirus homologue of the vaccinia F13 protein (VP37/p37, F13L gene), required for wrapping of the virion before release as an enveloped particle; it therefore blocks extracellular virus egress and spread.
